title: Heat illness: cool first, transport second
goal: Tell heat exhaustion from exertional heat stroke, confirm it with a rectal temperature, apply fast whole-body cooling, and explain what we know about return to play.

steps.title: Heat exhaustion or heat stroke?
steps.text:
Exercise in the heat raises [core temperature](g:core-temperature) ([hyperthermia](g:hyperthermia)); illness follows a spectrum. [Heat exhaustion](g:heat-exhaustion) is fatigue, weakness, dizziness, thirst and gut symptoms; it can precede heat stroke [[c:hi-exhaustion]]. [Exertional heat stroke](g:exertional-heat-stroke) (EHS) is the most severe form: core temperature above 40 °C **with** [CNS dysfunction](g:cns-dysfunction) [[c:hi-ehs]].

| | heat exhaustion | EHS |
|---|---|---|
| mind | clear, may be anxious | confused, irritable, collapse, odd behaviour |
| core temp | raised | above 40 °C |
| urgency | stop, cool, watch | emergency: cool at once |

EHS is one of the leading causes of sudden death in sport [[c:hi-death]]. The line between the two is the mind plus the temperature.

claims.text: Heat exhaustion is a spectrum of fatigue, weakness, dizziness and gastrointestinal symptoms, often a precursor to heat stroke.

evidence.quote: Heat exhaustion refers to a spectrum of symptoms that include fatigue, malaise, intense thirst, weakness, discomfort, anxiety, dizziness, and gastrointestinal symptoms, often a precursor to heat stroke

claims.text: Heat stroke is the most severe heat illness: core temperature above 40 °C with central nervous system dysfunction.

evidence.quote: Heatstroke represents the most severe form of heat-related illness and is characterized by core temperature above 40°C with central nervous system dysfunction.

claims.text: Exertional heat stroke remains one of the leading causes of sudden death during sport.

evidence.quote: exertional heat stroke remains one of the leading causes of sudden death during sport

steps.title: Diagnosis: take the rectal temperature
steps.text:
A collapsed, confused athlete must have core temperature measured **rectally**; it is more accurate than armpit, forehead, mouth or ear readings [[c:hi-rectal]]. In exercise in the heat those quick devices read on average 0.6–1.3 °C low [[c:hi-sites]], so a 38.9 °C armpit reading can hide a rectal temperature above 40 °C.

The rule: if the athlete is confused or collapsed in the heat, treat as EHS while you get the reading [[c:hi-suspect]].

Look-alikes (differentials only): [hyponatraemia](g:hyponatraemia) after heavy drinking, which also confuses [[c:hi-eah]], cardiac causes (heart modules), low blood sugar. Rectal temperature plus the story separates them.

claims.text: In the field a core temperature should be measured rectally, as more accurate than axillary, temporal, oral and aural readings.

evidence.quote: In the field setting, a core temperature should be measured rectally, as this is more accurate than axillary, temporal, oral, and aural temperature measurements.

claims.text: During exercise in the heat, oral, aural, temporal and axillary devices gave invalid, mostly too-low estimates of rectal temperature (about 0.6–1.3 °C).

evidence.quote: The following devices provided invalid estimates of rectal temperature: forehead sticker (0.29 degrees C [0.52 degrees F]), oral temperature using an inexpensive device (-1.13 degrees C [-2.03 degrees F]), temporal temperature measured according to the instruction manual (-0.87 degrees C [-1.56 degrees F]), temporal temperature using a modified technique (-0.63 degrees C [-1.13 degrees F]), oral temperature using an expensive device (-0.86 degrees C, [-1.55 degrees F]), aural temperature (-0.67 degrees C, [-1.20 degrees F]), axillary temperature using an inexpensive device (-1.25 degrees C, [-2.24 degrees F])

claims.text: Suspected EHS must be identified early and cooled at once: time is tissue.

evidence.quote: Identifying the athlete with suspected EHS early in the course, stopping activity (body heat generation), and providing rapid total body cooling are essential for survival, and like any critical life-threatening situation (cardiac arrest, brain stroke, sepsis), time is tissue.

claims.text: Exercise-associated hyponatraemia typically comes from drinking beyond sweat losses, and severe cases bring headache and confusion.

evidence.quote: Exercise-associated hyponatremia typically results from ingesting water or hypotonic beverages (including sports drinks) beyond sweat losses.
With the formation of cerebral edema at a plasma sodium concentration of <120 mmol/L, symptoms such as headache, confusion, agitation, coordination problems, and unconsciousness can occur

steps.title: Cool first, transport second
steps.text:
The treatment is fast, whole-body cooling: stop the activity and cool on the spot [[c:hi-time]]. The best method is [cold-water immersion](g:cold-water-immersion) (CWI) in a tub of cold or ice water, which cools fastest [[c:hi-cwi-fast]]. If no tub: keep dousing the athlete with water and fan them, while help arrives [[c:hi-alt]].

"Cool first, transport second" means start cooling before the ambulance ride, since outcome tracks how long severe hyperthermia lasts [[c:hi-duration]].

At the Falmouth Road Race, 274 EHS patients had CWI; the mean [cooling rate](g:cooling-rate) was 0.22 °C·min⁻¹ and all survived [[c:hi-survive]]. Eight more years added 180 cases: 454 in all, 100% survival [[c:hi-454]]. These are observational records (next card).

claims.text: Early recognition, stopping activity and rapid total body cooling are essential for survival of exertional heat stroke.

evidence.quote: Identifying the athlete with suspected EHS early in the course, stopping activity (body heat generation), and providing rapid total body cooling are essential for survival

Once heatstroke is recognized, treatment of heatstroke should be initiated immediately in the field, and Emergency Medical Services (EMS) should be activated for transportation of the patient to a medical treatment facility.

claims.text: Ice-water or cold-water immersion gives the fastest cooling for exertional hyperthermia.

evidence.quote: we concluded that ice-water immersion provides the most efficient cooling

claims.text: When immersion is not possible, continual dousing with water plus fanning is an alternative.

evidence.quote: continual dousing with water combined with fanning the patient is an alternative method

claims.text: EHS outcomes are likely related to how long severe hyperthermia lasts; time is tissue.

evidence.quote: Recovery from EHS is variable, and outcomes are likely related to the duration of severe hyperthermia.

claims.text: In 274 EHS patients treated with CWI at one race, mean cooling rate was 0.22 °C·min⁻¹ and survival was 100%.

evidence.quote: The average initial Tr was 41.44°C ± 0.63°C, and the average cooling rate for patients with EHS was 0.22°C·min ± 0.11°C·min.
CWI resulted in a 100% survival rate for all patients with EHS.

claims.text: With 180 more cases, the same race has 454 EHS cases with 100% survival under cold-water immersion.

evidence.quote: When combined with the previous dataset of EHS survivors from this race, it amounts to 454 EHS cases resulting in 100% survival.

steps.title: How long to cool?
steps.problem: A runner's rectal temperature is 41.4 °C. You aim to cool her to 39.0 °C at the mean CWI rate of 0.22 °C·min⁻¹. How many minutes?
steps: 2.4 ÷ 0.22 = 10.9 min, about 11 minutes. Real cooling varies (SD ±0.11 °C·min⁻¹), so keep measuring rather than trust the clock.

steps.title: How strong is the cooling evidence?
steps.text:
Nobody will randomise a collapsed athlete to no cooling, so the evidence is observational: case records from one well-staffed race [[c:hi-one-race]], a systematic review of a few cooling studies in exercise-induced hyperthermia [[c:hi-trials]], and expert consensus.

Limits to remember:

- The 100% survival comes from a race with a medical tent, rectal thermometers and tubs ready: it shows what is possible with fast CWI, not what happens everywhere.
- Cooling studies measured cooling speed in hot volunteers, not survival in true EHS.
- Survival also depends on how quickly cooling started, which a registry can't fully control.

The consensus view is still firm: rapid cooling is the cure, and prevention starts with well-known risk factors [[c:hi-prevent]].

claims.text: The Falmouth survival data are descriptive medical-tent records from one race, with no comparison group.

evidence.quote: Eighteen years of finish line medical tent patient records were obtained from the exertional heat illness treatment area at the Falmouth Road Race.
Descriptive epidemiologic study.

claims.text: The cooling review included only 7 of 89 articles and concluded on cooling rates in exercise-induced hyperthermia.

evidence.quote: Seven of 89 research articles met all inclusion criteria and a minimum score of 4 out of 10 on the PEDro scale.

Until future investigators identify other acceptable whole-body cooling modalities for exercise-induced hyperthermia, ice-water immersion and cold-water immersion are the methods proven to have the fastest cooling rates.

claims.text: Most exertional heat illnesses can be prevented by recognising and modifying well-described risk factors.

evidence.quote: Most exertional heat illnesses can be prevented with the recognition and modification of well-described risk factors

steps.title: Return to play
steps.text:
Recovery from EHS varies; outcomes seem tied to how long the severe hyperthermia lasted [[c:hi-recovery]]. A past EHS is itself a risk factor for another, so the return decision is hard [[c:hi-prior]].

Unlike rhabdomyolysis, EHS has return-to-activity guidelines in consensus statements (NATA, ACSM) [[c:hi-rtp-guides]], built on expert agreement more than trials. Some centres add a [heat tolerance test](g:heat-tolerance-test) (exercise in a controlled hot room); its role is still being worked out [[c:hi-htt]]. In practice: medical clearance first, then a stepwise return in load and heat (see [heat acclimation](g:heat-acclimation), heat module).

An athlete with heat exhaustion who does not recover quickly with rest and cooling is treated as a possible EHS.

claims.text: Recovery from exertional heat stroke is variable and likely related to the duration of severe hyperthermia.

evidence.quote: Recovery from EHS is variable, and outcomes are likely related to the duration of severe hyperthermia.

claims.text: A prior exertional heat stroke is an important risk factor for another, which makes return-to-play decisions challenging.

evidence.quote: Since current evidence suggests that the history of a prior event is an important risk factor for an EHS event, sports medicine providers can find post-EHS return to play/duty (RTP/D) decisions challenging.

claims.text: The NATA and ACSM consensus statements include return-to-activity guidance after exertional heat illness.

evidence.quote: The recommendations presented in this document provide athletic trainers and allied health providers with an integrated scientific and clinically applicable approach to the prevention, recognition, treatment of, and return-to-activity guidelines for EHIs.
Health care providers should be confident in the definitions, etiologies, and nuances of exertional heat exhaustion, exertional heat injury, and EHS.

claims.text: Heat tolerance testing can help with return decisions; its role is still being explored.

evidence.quote: Heat tolerance testing is a tool that can help with such decisions by exposing the subject to a given heat load under controlled conditions to assess the presence or absence of heat tolerance.
This special communication explores the challenge of the RTP/D after an EHS event and the potential role of heat tolerance testing in making this clinical decision.

points: Heat exhaustion: tired, dizzy, sick, mind clear. Heat stroke: core temperature above 40 °C with a confused or collapsed mind.
Measure rectal temperature; ear, mouth, armpit and forehead read too low.
Cool first, transport second: cold-water immersion cools fastest (about 0.22 °C·min⁻¹) and gave 100% survival in 454 race cases.
No tub: douse and fan. The evidence is observational but consistent and backed by consensus.
Return to play is individual: a past EHS is a risk factor for another.

variants.stem: What separates exertional heat stroke from heat exhaustion?

options.text: Core temperature above 40 °C with CNS dysfunction such as confusion
options.why: Correct: the mind and the temperature.

options.text: Heat stroke always comes with vomiting and diarrhoea
options.why: Gut symptoms occur in heat exhaustion too.

options.text: Heat stroke only occurs in the sun
options.why: It can occur whenever heat gain beats heat loss.

options.text: Heat stroke only happens once sweating has stopped
options.why: Not the marker: athletes with EHS are often still sweating.

variants.stem: In an Ironman run in 31 °C heat, athlete A is exhausted, dizzy and nauseated but answers questions normally. Athlete B is stumbling, irritable and gives odd answers. Whom do you treat as heat stroke first?

options.text: Athlete B: the changed mind suggests CNS dysfunction
options.why: Correct: confusion plus heat marks EHS until proven otherwise.

options.text: Athlete A: more tired
options.why: Fatigue and normal thinking fit exhaustion.

options.text: Neither until both vomit
options.why: Vomiting is not the criterion.

options.text: Both equally: temperature isn't needed
options.why: Rectal temperature is needed, and A's mind is clear.

variants.stem: A runner is confused after a hot 10 km. An ear thermometer reads 38.4 °C. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Unreliable: ear readings run low in the heat; take a rectal one
options.why: Correct: ear readings averaged about 0.7 °C low in exercise in the heat, and she is confused, so measure rectally.

options.text: Normal: she cannot have heat stroke
options.why: That would miss a true EHS.

options.text: Confirmed heat stroke: any reading above 38 °C
options.why: The criterion is above 40 °C with CNS signs.

options.text: Ignore temperature: mental state is enough
options.why: Mind and rectal temperature together decide.

variants.stem: A slow Ironman athlete who drank heavily is vomiting, headachy and confused at 22 °C. Why not just assume heat stroke?

options.text: Over-drinking can lower blood sodium, which also confuses
options.why: Correct: low blood sodium (hyponatraemia) from over-drinking can confuse too; a rectal temperature and the story help tell them apart (hydration module).

options.text: Heat stroke cannot occur at 22 °C
options.why: It can, which is why the rectal temperature matters; a normal one points elsewhere.

options.text: Confusion never occurs with low blood sodium
options.why: It does: brain swelling causes headache and confusion.

options.text: Vomiting rules out heat stroke
options.why: Vomiting occurs in heat illness and hyponatraemia alike.

variants.stem: A cyclist collapses, confused, in a time trial 40 min from a hospital. The race doctor has an ice-water tub. What first?

options.text: Cool in the tub on the spot, then transport
options.why: Correct: cool first, transport second.

options.text: Load him into the ambulance and cool at hospital
options.why: Each minute above 40 °C adds injury.

options.text: Give fluids and wait for a recovery
options.why: Fluids alone do not cool fast enough.

options.text: Take ear temperature and wait 20 min
options.why: Ear readings are invalid, and waiting delays cooling.

variants.stem: At a small road race there is no tub. A runner has suspected EHS. What is the best fallback?

options.text: Keep dousing with water and fanning while help comes
options.why: Correct: the review's alternative to immersion.

options.text: Wrap in a warm blanket to stop shaking
options.why: Raises heat; the opposite of cooling.

options.text: Walk him to the shade for 30 minutes
options.why: Too slow.

options.text: Give ice-cold sports drink only
options.why: Drinks do not cool the whole body fast.

variants.stem: A rectal temperature of 41.4 °C needs to be brought to 39.0 °C. The tub cools at 0.22 °C·min⁻¹. How many minutes?

options.text: 10.9 min
0.53 min
options.why: Multiplied degrees by rate instead of dividing.

options.text: 0.09 min
options.why: Divided rate by degrees: inverted.

options.text: 188 min
options.why: Divided the start temperature, forgetting the target.

variants.stem: A rectal temperature of 42.0 °C needs to be brought to 39.0 °C. The tub cools at 0.2 °C·min⁻¹. How many minutes?

options.text: 15.0 min
0.60 min
options.why: Multiplied degrees by rate instead of dividing.

options.text: 0.07 min
options.why: Divided rate by degrees: inverted.

options.text: 210 min
options.why: Divided the start temperature, forgetting the target.

variants.stem: A rectal temperature of 40.8 °C needs to be brought to 39.0 °C. The tub cools at 0.15 °C·min⁻¹. How many minutes?

options.text: 12.0 min
0.27 min
options.why: Multiplied degrees by rate instead of dividing.

options.text: 0.08 min
options.why: Divided rate by degrees: inverted.

options.text: 272 min
options.why: Divided the start temperature, forgetting the target.

variants.stem: The Falmouth cases show 100% survival with CWI. What most limits generalising to any race?

options.text: One well-equipped race tent and no comparison group
options.why: Correct: setting and no control group.

options.text: Observational data can never say anything about treatment
options.why: Too strong: large, consistent case series plus cooling-rate studies do inform practice.

options.text: The sample was only 20 people
options.why: Hundreds of cases: the sample is large.

options.text: Rectal temperature was not measured
options.why: It was: mean 41.44 °C.

variants.stem: Which fact makes return to play after exertional heat stroke hard to decide?

options.text: A prior event is an important risk factor for another
options.why: Correct: the source states this.

options.text: Heat stroke is always fatal
options.why: Survival is high with fast cooling.

options.text: There is a single test that clears everyone
options.why: Heat tolerance testing is debated.

options.text: Athletes always recover within a week
options.why: Recovery varies.

variants.stem: A runner had heat stroke 3 weeks ago and feels fine. He wants to race a hot half marathon next week. Best judgement?

options.text: Not yet: get medical clearance and return step by step
options.why: Correct: a prior EHS raises risk, and feeling fine does not remove it.

options.text: Fine: feeling well shows he has fully recovered
options.why: Recovery varies, and a prior EHS is a risk factor.

options.text: Fine if he drinks more
options.why: Fluids don't remove the risk.

options.text: He should never run in the heat again
options.why: Too strong; return is possible with guidance.
